fields.Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "Separating God from religion", "body": "Matthew Hutchison, who streams as Lord Bear 33 and is 22, tells Chance Garton he came out of a hard atheist upbringing and reverted to Islam, and that his quarrel is not with God but with religion as an institution. In his account a prophet arrives, and a century later the authorities he calls Pharisees build something around that prophet he never taught, a pattern he says runs through Judaism, Christianity and Islam alike. He says he holds no dogmatic view, is looking at all three from the outside, and sees an effort under way to set believers against each other."}, {"title": "The fitra and doing good for good's sake", "body": "Matthew introduces the fitra, which in his account is the built in natural state a person has when left untampered with, and he argues that much of modern life, from the calendar to the phone in a young person's hand, is designed to pull people off it. Chance Garton takes the thread into morality, saying the wages of sin are simply the natural ramifications of acting out of alignment with nature, so no thunderbolt from Zeus is required. Both prefer teaching that answers why over religious law delivered as because I said so, and agree that good carries its own reward."}, {"title": "Victim consciousness and the role of the adversary", "body": "Matthew argues that the victim mindset, not an outside enemy, is the real trouble, since endless complaint breeds subservience and quietly makes an idol of whoever you blame. Chance Garton notes that the word victim originally meant a sacrificial offering, and questions any hero model built on self sacrifice, because a collective that sacrifices everyone has sacrificed itself. Both keep returning to the detail Matthew raises, that in the Quran Satan asks permission before rebelling, reading the adversary as opposition that strengthens rather than a boogeyman to blame. Gabe, the co-host, adds that martyr and witness share a root."}, {"title": "Scripture written in the sky", "body": "Chance Garton traces astro theology through both books, from Godfrey Higgins and his Neros cycle of roughly 600 to 650 years between incarnations of the firstborn of the first cause, to Quran 43:4 and 85:22, which he says describe a celestial tablet in heaven, and the meaning of Quran as recital. He reads the tradition that Salman al Farsi, a slave Magi, taught the Prophet as a fingerprint of the captured astrologer, the same category as Homer and Daniel, and recommends John McHugh's book The Celestial Code of Scripture. Matthew adds that Quranic verses on the stars address those who understand the sky."}, {"title": "Intention, identity and kicking addictions", "body": "In the closing stretch Chance Garton raises niyyah, the intention stated in the heart before prayer, and ties it to the harder question of what a person actually wants once temporary sensory wants are cleared away. Matthew says a year of adding the works to the faith cleared out every addiction he had, right down to the last one. Chance argues that addiction leans on an untrue story attached to identity, which is why he finds the twenty year I am an alcoholic label insidious, and they close on marriage as a starting point rather than a Hollywood finish line."}]
fields.Intro Paragraph 1: Matthew Hutchison, aka LordBear33, joins Vibe Rant to share his perspective on the value systems of Islam. As an individual who took up the practice by choice, Matthew has valuable insights into the morality of this religion, and what westerners tend to misunderstand about its laws. He's also the founder of Dawahgram, a Halal social media platform that's been growing rapidly.
